Loss = mean squared miss of the slope. Backprop nudges all weights so that miss gets smaller. Nothing else is graded. Idea from: Flow Matching (Lipman et al., 2022), the loss on v.
Chapter E5b The first idea most people have: give the noisy image, predict the clean image x.

Why not just predict the image x with a normal MSE?

  1. Your idea: the model outputs x_hat

    Give the model the noisy image and let it output the clean image x_hat. The loss is a normal MSE: mean((x_hat − x)²). This is a real method.

  2. Ours: the model outputs v

    The model outputs the slope v. We get the image with x_hat = noisy − t·v. The loss is mean((v − (eps − x))²). Both ways end in the same picture.

  3. The two losses differ by exactly t²

    The miss in x is t times the miss in v. So the loss in x is t² times ours. On frame 326, t = 0.60 and the ratio is 0.36.

    —x-loss / v-loss, measured
  4. What t² means for each frame

    At t = 0.1 the x-loss counts a frame 0.01 times as much as the v-loss. Ours weighs lightly noised questions more.

  5. Why we predict the slope

    Play walks along the line in steps: z = z + (t_next − t)·v. A step needs exactly the slope. It is also the standard rectified-flow recipe.

  6. Predicting x also works

    A 2025 paper (JiT) shows that predicting x also works for pixel models. Here it is a choice of bookkeeping, not a different idea.

Same noisy image in, same clean picture out. Only the weight of each frame in the loss changes, by t². Idea from: Rectified Flow (Liu et al., 2022), Flow Matching (Lipman et al., 2022); JiT (Li & He, 2025).
Chapter E6 What play does with the slope. Training does it differently.

How does play draw a new frame from pure noise?

  1. Start from pure noise

    There is no real frame to hide, so play starts from torch.randn. This picture sits at t = 1.0. Its mean miss against the real frame 326 is 94.8 out of 255.

  2. Pass 1: the model gives a slope

    The model sees the noise, the past 15 frames and the key. It outputs v1. The slope picture looks like noise, but it holds the way back.

  3. Take half the walk

    Play steps by t_next − t = 0.5 − 1.0, so z = z + (t_next − t)·v. Half of the noise is removed. Nobody adds noise. The miss falls to 48.2.

  4. Pass 2: ask again at t = 0.5

    The same model gets the half-clean picture and t = 0.5. It outputs v2. This is a new question, at a new noise level.

  5. The last half of the walk

    Step by 0 − 0.5 along v2. That gives the new frame. Its miss against the real frame is 0.7 out of 255.

  6. Training asks once

    Training never walks. It hides frame 326 at one random t, gets one slope, grades it against eps − x, and stops. Then it adjusts the weights.

Play walks 1.0 → 0.5 → 0.0 in two passes. Training asks one question per frame at one random t. Both use the same slope. Idea from: Rectified Flow (Liu et al., 2022), walking back along the line in a few steps.
Chapter F1 Fail first: what goes wrong if the past is always perfect.

Why do we noise the past at all?

  1. In play the past is drawn by the model

    The left picture is a real frame. The middle one is the model's own redraw of it. They look the same, but the right picture shows the small differences, brightened 20 times.

  2. Fail first: a perfect past in training

    Suppose training only ever shows real frames as the past. Then play hands the model a past it has never seen. Each small error becomes the next frame's input. This sketch is an idea, not a measurement.

  3. The fix: noise the past by a random amount

    Each past frame gets noise t_c, drawn between 0 and 0.35. These are real pictures of one window. At 0.001 the frame is clean. At 0.311 it is clearly noisy.

  4. Play's 0.05 is inside the range

    Play always uses 0.05 for the past. Training saw every amount from 0 to 0.35, so 0.05 is familiar. Each dot is one real t_c from this window.

  5. The model is told t_c

    The model gets t_c with each past frame. So it can tell a clean past from a noisy one. The idea is that it then relies less on fine detail. This is not measured.

A slightly noisy past teaches the model to ignore small mistakes. Play's own drawings then do not push it off course. Idea from: GameNGen (Valevski et al., 2024), noise augmentation on the past.
Chapter F2 One real window of 16 frames, made into two copies.

What are the two copies of one window, and what is each for?

  1. One real window

    Take 16 frames in a row from one game: frames 319 to 334. Under each frame is the key that produced it. Frame 326 has key 1, a tap.

  2. Copy one: the clean copy, the past

    Each frame is noised a little, by its own t_c from 0 to 0.35. This is the past as play will see it. It is never perfectly clean.

  3. Copy two: the noisy copy, the questions

    Each frame is noised by t_n, a random number from 0 to 1. Noisy position 9 is built from real position 9 itself, not from position 8. The exact eps is kept.

  4. Follow one pixel at position 9

    The clean value uses t_c = 0.311. The noisy value uses t_n = 0.794. The noise of the clean copy is thrown away. The eps of the noisy copy is kept for the answer.

  5. The code, loss.py:13-24

    The two lines with mix are the same formula. They differ in the job. Clean is the past. Noisy is the question.

  6. Both noise levels go into the model

    The call passes clean, t_c, noisy and t_n. The model needs t_n because the right slope changes with t. It needs t_c to know how far to trust the past.

Same mix, two jobs. The clean copy is the past it reads. The noisy copy is the set of questions it must answer. Idea from: Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025), teacher forcing; Diffusion Forcing (Chen et al., 2024); SD3 (Esser et al., 2024), t.
Chapter F2b Two noise numbers, two kinds of frame, training and play.

Which noise number belongs to which frame, in training and in play?

  1. Training, the past: t_c from 0 to 0.35

    The past frames get t_c = rand * 0.35. The blue band shows the range. The dots are the 16 real t_c values of the window on the last page.

  2. Play, the past: always 0.05

    When play pushes a frame, it uses 0.05. That sits inside the blue band. So the model has met this noise level in training.

  3. Training, the frame being drawn: t_n from 0 to 1

    The noisy copy gets t_n = sigmoid(randn). Most values are medium. Half of them fall between 0.34 and 0.66. Only 1.4% are below 0.1.

  4. Play, the frame being drawn: 1.0, 0.5, 0.0

    Play starts at pure noise and removes noise in two passes. Nobody adds noise at 0.5. The picture simply is at 0.5 after pass 1.

  5. Do not mix the rows

    The 0.60 on earlier pages is one dot in the bottom left box. The range 0 to 0.35 belongs only to the past. The range 0 to 1 belongs only to the frame being drawn.

Past frames get a little noise. The frame being drawn gets any amount. Training covers every level that play will use. Idea from: Diffusion Forcing (Chen et al., 2024); GameNGen (Valevski et al., 2024); SD3 (Esser et al., 2024).
Chapter F3 32 frames in one pass: 16 clean, then 16 noisy.

Which frames may each frame read?

  1. A 32 × 32 grid of frames

    Each row is a frame that reads. Each column is a frame that may be read. The order is C0 to C15, then N0 to N15. Grey means blocked.

  2. Clean frame i reads clean 0 … i

    The blue triangle is the clean copy. It reads itself and the clean frames before it. This is exactly what a push does in play.

  3. Noisy frame i reads clean 0 … i−1, and itself

    Each orange row reads the clean frames before it. It also reads its own noisy frame. This is exactly what a draw does in play.

  4. Follow noisy position 9

    Noisy 9 reads clean 0 to 8 and itself. It must not read clean 9. That is the same frame, only lightly noised, so it would give away the answer.

  5. 272 of 1,024 pairs are allowed

    That is 26.6% of the grid. The rule is the function can_read in world.py:11-20. The other 73.4% of pairs get zero share.

    272of 1,024 frame pairs
    26.6%allowed
Each noisy frame sees what play would show it. Only a clean past, plus itself. Nothing from its own answer. Idea from: Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025), its Teacher Forcing baseline; Causal Forcing, clean and noisy copies with one mask.
Chapter F4 The whole training pass, with the shape after each step.

How does one pass ask 16 questions at once?

  1. 32 frames become 8,192 rows

    Clean C0 to C15 and noisy N0 to N15 sit in one list. Each frame has 256 squares, so each frame is 256 rows of 768 numbers. One window is 32 × 256 = 8,192 rows.

  2. 16 blocks, with the can_read rule

    All 8,192 rows go through the 16 blocks together. The grid from the last page decides who reads whom. The shape does not change.

  3. Keep only the noisy half

    The model uses x[:, T:], the last 16 frames. The clean half only served as memory. It gets no output and no grade. That is world.py:84-96.

    16questions per window
    128per step, 8 windows
  4. Slopes out, then the loss

    The head gives 256 × 192 numbers per frame. They fold into a 3 × 128 × 128 picture of slopes. Each one is graded against eps − x.

  5. Each question has its own t

    Every noisy frame has its own t_n. So the 16 questions ask about 16 different noise levels in one pass. Play draws at two levels, 1.0 and 0.5.

One pass, 16 questions, one grade per noisy frame. Training asks each frame once. It never walks like play does. Idea from: Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025), its Teacher Forcing baseline, all frames in one pass.
Chapter G1 The loss is one number. This page shows what happens to the weights next.

After the loss, how does one update change the model?

  1. A batch becomes one number

    In the real run one batch is 8 windows of 16 frames. The model guesses a slope for every pixel. The loss averages all the misses into one number.

    The numbers on steps 1 to 4 come from a small demo model: 758,848 weights, one 4-frame window.

    1.2907loss of the small demo model, step 0
  2. backward: one gradient for each weight

    First zero_grad forgets the last step. Then loss.backward() gives every weight its own gradient. A gradient says which way the loss moves if that weight goes up.

    Follow one weight of the demo model: out.weight[0,0]. Its gradient is +0.0000469, so raising it would raise the loss.

  3. Clip: keep the push small

    All gradients together have one length. If that length is above 1.0, they are all shrunk until it is exactly 1.0. In stage 1, 2 of the 296 logged values went above the line. We log every 100th step.

  4. AdamW moves every weight a little

    Each weight moves against its gradient. Our demo weight goes from +0.0000000 to −0.0009998. The demo learning rate was 0.001 with no warmup, so the first move is about that size. The real run uses 0.0002. AdamW uses betas 0.9 and 0.95 and weight decay 0.01.

    758,848demo weights moved at once (the real model: 172,518,848)
  5. Warmup: tiny steps first

    The first gradients are junk, so the learning rate starts at zero. It climbs in a straight line to 0.0002 over 1,000 steps. Then it stays there.

  6. Repeat, and the loss falls

    Next window, next noise, same four moves. The demo model goes from 1.29 to 0.35 in 1,500 steps. The real model reaches 0.00055 at the last logged step, 29,500.

  7. Two one-line speedups

    Under autocast the maths runs in bf16, which is faster on the GPU. And torch.compile wraps the loss once. Neither changes the idea above.

The next step after backprop is the update. Gradients say which way, clipping keeps the push small, and AdamW moves every weight. Repeat that and the loss falls. Idea from: AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017); gradient clipping by total norm (Pascanu et al., 2013); learning-rate warmup (Goyal et al., 2017).
Chapter G2 The EMA is part of our own run. It is not another model.

How is the shadow copy of the model made?

  1. Copy the model once, at step 0

    In stage 1 both copies start from the same random weights, so nothing comes from a finished model. The real numbers on this page come from a small demo model of 758,848 weights. The copy gets no gradients, so it never learns by itself.

  2. After every step, the shadow follows

    The model takes its AdamW step. Then each shadow weight moves a small part of the way toward the model weight. The rule is ema = d * ema + (1 - d) * model.

  3. Follow one demo weight at step 400

    The shadow was at the old value. The model weight has moved on. The shadow takes only 2.2% of the distance and stays close to where it was.

  4. The share d changes with the step

    At step 1 the shadow moves 82% of the way, so it can leave the random start. In the 600-step demo, d only reaches 0.985. In the real run d reaches 0.9995 near step 18,000.

    0.9995d from about step 18,000 on
  5. Six hundred steps of one demo weight

    The grey line is the model weight. It wobbles because each step uses one random batch. The blue shadow follows a little behind and stays smooth.

  6. Play and the checks use the shadow

    At the end of training we save both copies. The EMA file is the one we load to play the game. The next page shows why.

The EMA is a running average of our own weights. It is one extra copy, pulled a little toward the model after every step. Idea from: EMA of the weights (Polyak & Juditsky, 1992, averaging), used for diffusion sampling in DDPM (Ho et al., 2020).
Chapter G3 The shadow copy costs one extra copy. Here is what it buys.

Why do we need the shadow copy at all?

  1. The model weights jitter

    Every AdamW step is pushed by one random batch. So the weights keep jumping around a good spot. Look at the second half of a small demo run: 3,000 steps of the 758,848-weight model. The grey model loss on 64 held-out windows zig-zags.

  2. The shadow averages the jitter away

    The blue shadow copy goes smoothly through the middle of the zig-zag. Here it beat the model at 24 of the 31 checks in this zoom. In this short run d is 0.997, so it averages about the last 334 steps. In the real run d is 0.9995, about 2,000 steps.

  3. Early on, the shadow is worse

    On the whole run the two lines look the same. But from step 50 to 500 the shadow lags behind a model that still improves fast.

    After step 1,550 it is a little better. Its loss jumps about two thirds as much between checks.

    0.00044average jump of the shadow loss (model: 0.00068)
  4. The real run: the gap is big

    On the small run the gain is tiny, 0.4082 against 0.4088. On our full stage-1 run it is clear. At step 28,000 the model scores 0.00074 and the shadow scores 0.00039, about half.

    1.9xlower held-out loss with the shadow copy
  5. So we play with the shadow

    The loss we train on is the model's. The weights we keep, play and check are the shadow's. The shadow never gets gradients, so it costs one extra copy.

The shadow copy is the steadier model. It lags early, but at step 28,000 of the real run its held-out loss is about half of the model's. Idea from: EMA of the weights (Polyak & Juditsky, 1992, averaging), used for diffusion sampling in DDPM (Ho et al., 2020).
Chapter G4 Fail first. We run the same loop on a tiny model on the laptop.

What happens when the model is too small?

  1. A model 227 times smaller

    The small model has 2 blocks and width 128. That is 758,848 learned numbers. The real model has 172,518,848, so the small one is 0.44% of its size.

    758,848learned numbers, against 172,518,848
  2. Same loop, 1,500 steps

    We train it on one window of 4 real frames from a training game, again and again. The loss falls fast from 1.29 and then stalls near 0.35.

  3. One fixed question

    We hide frame 326 behind noise at level 0.6. Then we ask the model for the clean frame. The left picture is the real frame, and the second is the noisy one it sees.

  4. The small model draws noise

    At step 0 it outputs zero, so we see the noisy frame back. At step 1,500 the scene shows, but it is still covered in noise. The miss is the average gap per pixel and colour, 33 on a 0 to 255 scale.

    33 / 255average pixel miss after 1,500 steps
  5. The real model on the same question

    Our final stage-3 model answers with a clean frame. Its miss is 0.20 out of 255. Its loss on this question is 0.00013, against 0.35 for the small one.

    0.20 / 255average pixel miss, stage-3 model
The small model learns the loop and stalls. This is not a controlled size test. The big model trained for tens of thousands of steps on many games, and this frame is from a training game. Held-out loss is on page G5. Idea from: Rectified Flow (Liu et al., 2022), the slope the small model must learn; the size test is standard practice.
Chapter G5 The same loop, with the real model, on a real GPU.

How does the loss of our stage 1 fall on the GPU?

  1. Stage 1 on GPU 7

    We trained the full 172.5M model from random weights on one H100. It ran for 121 minutes at about 0.246 seconds per step. That gave 29,525 steps, using 56.1 GB of memory.

    29,525steps in 121 minutes
  2. The training loss falls more than 3 orders

    The loss starts at 1.28, the same as the small model. At the last logged step it is 0.00055, about 2,300 times lower. The line wobbles because every step uses a new batch.

  3. The held-out loss falls smoothly

    Every 2,000 steps we score windows from games the model never trained on. These dots fall smoothly. They sit on or a little above the training loss, which is what we expect for games it never saw.

  4. The shadow copy is lower again

    The dashed line is the shadow copy on the same windows. At step 28,000 the model scores 0.00074 and the shadow scores 0.00039.

    0.00039held-out loss of the shadow copy, step 28,000
Stage 1 trains smoothly. The loss falls from 1.28 to 0.00055, and the shadow copy ends at about half the model's held-out loss. Play checks come next. Idea: standard practice (train from scratch, score held-out games, keep the EMA copy).
Chapter H1 Live play must draw a frame fast. Here is the cost of the first idea.

Why not read the whole past again for every new frame?

  1. First idea: re-read all 15 past frames

    For every new frame, push the 15 past frames through the 16 blocks again. Each frame is 256 rows. So that is 15 x 256 rows, plus 2 passes of 256 rows for the new frame.

    4,352rows through the 16 blocks, per new frame
  2. Better: keep the past, do only the new work

    A finished frame never changes. So we save its k and v once, on the shelf. Then each new frame costs 2 passes to draw and 1 pass to save: 3 x 256 rows.

    768rows per new frame, with the shelf
  3. Do the multiply: what is on the shelf

    A frame is 128 x 128 pixels. Squares of 8 pixels give 16 x 16 = 256 squares, so 256 rows. 15 frames give 15 x 256 = 3,840 rows.

    Every block saves k and v for those rows, each 768 numbers wide. The shelf is the kept k and v of all 16 blocks. That is 16 x 3,840 x 768 for k, and the same again for v.

  4. The past is read in one place only

    Each block's 256 new rows read 3,840 rows from that block's part of the shelf, plus their own 256. That is 4,096 rows, inside attention in every block. No past frame is ever added to the noise as pixels.

The shelf means 5.7 times fewer rows through the blocks. It holds 94,371,840 numbers, and the new frame reads it inside attention. Idea from: CausVid (Yin et al., 2024), keep k and v of past frames (KV cache) for frame-by-frame video.
Chapter H2 The shelf holds the past. Two moves use it: push and draw.

How do push and draw fill and read the shelf?

  1. The shelf is a grid

    The shelf is the kept k and v of all 16 blocks. Draw it as 16 layers, one per block, and 15 columns, one per past frame. Each cell holds that block's k and v for the 256 rows of that frame. One block's part of the shelf has k and v of shape [B, 12, 3840, 64]. Blocks are counted from 1.

  2. Push: save a finished frame

    First we add 0.05 noise to the pixels of the frame. Then one pass runs through the 16 blocks. Each block writes its k and v into a new column, and the oldest column drops out.

    The noise goes on the picture, never on k or v. The head output of this pass is thrown away.

  3. Draw: make the next frame

    We start from pure noise. Pass 1 goes from t = 1.0 to 0.5, and pass 2 from 0.5 to 0.0. Both passes read the shelf. The shelf does not change during a draw.

  4. One real draw, in pictures

    Pass 1 asks the model for a slope. We take half a step back along it: z minus 0.5 times v. Pass 2 does the same from half noise.

    No new noise is added while drawing. The pixel miss falls from 94.8 to 48.0 to 0.72 out of 255. In stage 1 there is one pass and the model never draws. In stages 2 and 3 the EMA copy redraws two frames of each window.

  5. Three passes for each frame

    The finished frame has not run through the blocks yet. So one more pass makes its k and v. Pass 2 only saw a half-noisy picture.

    In training the past gets a random noise level from 0 to 0.35. Our 0.05 sits inside that range. Streaming costs 3 passes of 256 rows.

  6. The model holds no score and no crash rule

    It draws the score digit as pixels, like the pipes. A separate pixel check ends the game. The bird counts as found with 3 orange pixels, and 3 missed frames in a row end the run. The play checks draw with 4 passes, these pages show 2.

    The next part follows one real look-up through the shelf with real numbers.

Push writes the shelf. Draw reads it. Each frame uses 2 draw passes and 1 push pass, all of them 256 rows through 16 blocks. Idea from: CausVid (Yin et al., 2024), KV cache; GameNGen (Valevski et al., 2024), noise on the past.
Chapter H3 Rotating q and k by position, and why q·k depends only on m − n, is on page C3.

Why must a saved key be un-rotated, and what is pos=None?

  1. m and n in the play loop

    The shelf holds the last 15 frames. The oldest is at position 0 and the newest at 14. The frame being drawn is at 15, as streamer.py:24 says.

    Each frame has 256 squares, so each position is used for 256 keys. Click any frame to follow it.

  2. Slide the window: every position drops by one

    Move the slider by one. The oldest frame leaves, and every other frame moves down by one position. Frame 318 goes from position 7 to 6, 5, 4 and so on.

  3. Save the key rotated, or un-rotated?

    Row B saves k already rotated, once, when the frame was saved. It was the frame in hand then, so it was rotated by 15. It is never rotated again.

    Row A saves k plain and rotates it at each use. So m − n is always the true number of frames back.

  4. That is why pos=None

    Inside the block, block.py:35-36 would rotate only the 256 new keys. With pos=None the block skips it and hands k back plain at line 41.

    Then attention, called at line 37, glues the shelf on and rotates all 4,096 keys with pos_all.

  5. One whole pass, with real shapes

    This is _pass for one frame, batch size 1. The yellow rows are the ones that matter for this trap. Every pass, 4,096 keys are rotated in each block.

    94.4 Mnumbers saved on the shelf
A saved key must not carry a position. The window slides, so the position must be counted again at every pass. Idea from: RoFormer (Su et al., 2021), RoPE; CausVid (Yin et al., 2024), the KV cache.
Chapter H4 We built the wrong version on purpose and played both on real frames.

Can one drawn frame show the trap?

  1. Draw one frame both ways

    We push 15 real frames into an empty shelf. Then we draw frame 313 with plain keys, and again with keys rotated at push. Both miss the real frame by about 0.7 out of 255.

    The shelf was still filling, so the rotated keys carry 0 to 14. Those are the correct offsets for this first draw. The two designs are the same maths here, so one frame cannot tell them apart.

    1.24miss, plain keys, out of 255
    1.24miss, rotated at push
  2. Where does one real frame look?

    The bars show how much the frame being drawn looks at each saved frame. It is our stage-3 model on real frames, drawing frame 326 after 28 pushes. We look at block 9 of 16, counted from 1.

    Plain keys: it looks most at itself and the newest frames, then less and less. We read this as how it sees the bird's speed. We did not test that.

  3. Rotated at push: every frame looks the same

    The window has slid by now. Almost every saved key was rotated by 15 when it was saved, and the two oldest by 13 and 14. So they look about 0 frames back. The bars are flat, and old and new look the same.

  4. Draw 30 frames in a row

    Now each drawn frame goes back on the shelf, as in real play. Plain keys follow the real game. Rotated keys draw a bird that does not move. The window slides, and that is the whole trap.

  5. The bird height tells the truth

    The line is the bird's height in each frame. Plain keys stay on the real line. Rotated keys stay at row 59 to 60 for all 30 frames.

One frame cannot see the bug. Thirty frames can. A test for memory must run many frames and watch the bird. Idea from: RoFormer (Su et al., 2021), RoPE. The 30-frame test is ours.
The memory, 1 of 3 Page H3 explains why keys stay plain. This page only counts. Blocks are counted 1 to 16; the code counts 0 to 15.

How many numbers does the memory hold?

  1. One frame is 256 rows

    A frame is 128 × 128 pixels. We cut it into squares of 8 × 8 pixels, 16 across and 16 down. That gives 16 × 16 = 256 squares. Each square becomes one row of 768 numbers.

    256rows in one frame
  2. 15 frames are 3,840 rows

    The memory holds the last 15 frames. Each frame is 256 rows, and the frames sit one after the other. So 15 × 256 = 3,840 rows. We call this the past table.

    3,840rows in the past table
  3. One block saves two tables

    The 15 frames go through the 16 blocks in one batch. Live play pushes them one at a time. It makes the same v, and the same k before the turn by position. Each block keeps k and v, each 3,840 × 768, which is 2,949,120 numbers.

  4. 16 blocks keep 16 shelves

    Every block keeps its own pair, so there are 16 shelves. For k alone, 16 × 3,840 × 768 = 47,185,920 numbers. The tables for v have the same size.

    47,185,920numbers in k
    47,185,920numbers in v
  5. Together: 94,371,840 numbers

    Add k and v: 47,185,920 + 47,185,920 = 94,371,840. Count it another way: 15 frames in 16 blocks make 240 saved pieces. Each piece is a k and a v of 256 × 768, so 480 tables.

    94,371,840numbers in the whole memory
  6. A block reads 4,096 rows

    The new frame is only 256 rows. Block n reads its own 3,840 saved rows and these 256 new rows. So 3,840 + 256 = 4,096 rows, each of 768 numbers.

    4,096rows one block reads
The memory is 16 × 2 × 3,840 × 768 = 94,371,840 numbers. The next page shows where each saved row comes from. Idea from: CausVid (Yin et al., 2024), saved k and v reused frame by frame.
The memory, 2 of 3 Pages H2 and H3 explain the shelf and why keys stay plain. Here we see where the shelves come from. Blocks are counted 1 to 16.

Where do the saved rows come from?

  1. Run 1: 15 past frames, one batch

    These pictures read the 15 past frames in one batch. Each frame gets a little noise (t = 0.05) and is cut into 256 squares. 15 × 256 = 3,840 rows. Live play pushes one frame at a time and builds the same tables.

    3,840rows in the past table
  2. Block 1 saves its k and v

    The 3,840 rows enter block 1. Block 1 makes q, k and v for every row, 3,840 rows each. It puts k and v on shelf 1. That is what "saved" means. These k pictures are turned by position. Live play stores k plain (page H3).

  3. Block 2 saves its own pair

    Block 1 also runs attention and its MLP on the past table, so the table changes. The changed table enters block 2. Block 2 makes its own k and v, with its own weights, for shelf 2.

  4. All 16 blocks do the same

    Every block fills one shelf. So 16 shelves × 15 frames = 240 saved pieces, each 256 rows. Shelf n holds the k and v that block n made from the table entering block n. The table after block 16 is never used.

    16shelves
    3,840rows on each
  5. Run 2: the new frame reads shelf 1

    The new frame is a table of only 256 rows. Here it is the half-noisy frame (t = 0.5, key 0) that enters draw pass 2. Block 1 makes its own q, k and v. K is shelf 1's k with the new k below it, 4,096 rows, and V is built the same way. This stacking is the look-up.

  6. Every block reads its own shelf

    Block 2 reads shelf 2, block 9 reads shelf 9, and so on. Each shelf was made by the same block in run 1. So the past enters the new frame 16 times, once in each block.

  7. The new frame joins the shelves

    After block 16, the head turns the 256 rows into pixels: the new frame. Live play then pushes it at once, in one pass at t = 0.05. Its 256 rows join every shelf, and the oldest frame's 256 rows leave.

The past enters only through the shelves. Each frame fills its band once, by a push. Run 2 reads them in every block. Idea from: CausVid (Yin et al., 2024), saved k and v reused frame by frame.
The memory, 3 of 3 Real numbers: the bird's square, block 9, head 12 (counted from 1; code index 8 and 11). The frame is half noise (t = 0.5, key 0), as it enters draw pass 2.

Where are the past frames read?

  1. Two separate tables

    The 15 past frames make a tall blue table of 3,840 rows. The new frame makes a short red table of 256 rows. It is half noise (t = 0.5). Both are drawn to scale. Nothing from the past is added to its pixels.

  2. Earlier, block 9 saved k and v

    These tables come from one batch read of the 15 frames. Live play pushes them one at a time. Block 9 kept k for matching and v for content, 3,840 rows each. Its k is turned by position here; play stores it plain (page H3).

  3. Now: new q, k, v, then stack

    The new table reaches block 9. Its 256 rows make q (the question of each square), k and v. The saved rows go on top of the new rows, so K and V have 4,096 rows. This stacking is the only place the past enters.

    3,840saved rows
    256new rows
  4. One square asks: the bird

    Take row 132 of q, the bird's square. Its 64 numbers are compared with all 4,096 rows of K, and each score is divided by 8. Softmax turns the scores into shares that add up to 1.

    92.1%of the shares on past rows
    7.9%on the new frame
  5. Where those shares sit

    Each share belongs to one square of one frame. Drawn back on the pictures, the biggest sit on past frames 15 and 14. They are at square 131, next to the bird's square 132. Past frame 15 is the newest of the 15.

    37.4%past frame 15, square 131
    17.3%past frame 14, square 131
  6. Take that much of each v row

    Each of the 4,096 v rows has 64 numbers. Multiply each row by its share, then add up all the rows. The five biggest parts are shown. The sum is the bird's new 64 numbers for this head.

  7. The mix is added to the bird's row

    All 12 heads do this. Their 12 × 64 results join into 768 numbers, pass through proj, and are scaled by the gate. The result is added to the bird's row, so the new table now carries the past. Block 10 repeats this with its own shelf.

The look-up is one line: out = shares · V. The past frames never go back in as pictures. Their saved rows are read inside every block. Idea from: Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), attention shares; CausVid (Yin et al., 2024), saved k and v.
Chapter J1 Training is done. Now we need to know if the world works.

How do we know the world works, not only that the loss is low?

  1. The loss looks perfect

    After stage 1 the held-out loss is tiny. But the loss always reads a real past. In play the model reads its own drawings. So we let it play and measure.

    0.00039loss, EMA copy
    6%bird found, frames 101-200
  2. Check A: where is the bird?

    We find the bird as the orange pixels and take their average row. The model draws 300 frames with the real keys. Each frame, we compare its bird row with the real bird row.

  3. Check B: does a pipe appear?

    We pick 256 moments where a new pipe enters on the right. The model starts 4 frames early and draws 5 frames. We count green pixels in the yellow strip. A pass needs 30% of the real green. A short clip may not show a failure, so we test many moments. Stage 1 and stage 3 are two models of ours, explained later.

  4. Check C: can it play alone?

    In a free dream an auto-pilot taps toward the gap, so no real key helps. The dream runs all 1,000 frames. The loss frame is the first time the bird is missing for 3 frames. A wall is a pipe with no gap of 12 sky rows.

  5. Read each number against the real game

    A number alone means little. The real game is the target. By definition its bird miss is 0 and its pipe score is 100%. Survival is capped at 1,000, so more is better.

A low loss is not a working world. Only letting the model play on its own drawings shows if the bird and the pipes survive. Idea: ours (the three play checks).
Chapter J2 The same three checks, run on stage 1 at three points in its training.

Is stage 1 good, and what does it get wrong?

  1. Five numbers, three checkpoints

    We saved stage 1 at steps 6,604, 14,169 and 29,525. Each bar is one checkpoint, with the first in grey. Green means better than the checkpoint before. Red means worse. Each bar is one run, so small changes may be noise.

  2. Pipes and bird position improve

    Later checkpoints have fewer wall frames and a smaller bird miss. At 6,604 the bird misses by 2.02 px. At 29,525 it misses by 0.135 px. But the bird is found less and less.

  3. See it in free dreams

    These are real dreams of the final checkpoint. Green frames still show the bird. The dream runs on after the bird is lost, with pipes only. The loss never showed this.

  4. Two things stay wrong

    The bird is found in only 6% of frames 101-200. A new pipe appears after 4 own frames in 84.4% of cases, and the real game gives 100%.

    6%bird found
    84.4%new pipe appears
Stage 1 beats its early checkpoints on pipes and walls, but it loses the bird and misses about 1 new pipe in 6. Check more than the last checkpoint: the early one found the bird more often, but drew it badly. Idea from: GameNGen (Valevski et al., 2024), run the model on its own frames and look at the drift.
Chapter K1 Stage 1 loses the bird in long play. Here is why.

Why does the bird get lost when the model plays alone?

  1. In training the past is always real

    Each training window has 16 real frames. Each frame is asked from the real frames before it, lightly noised. It never reads a picture that it drew itself.

  2. In play the past is its own drawing

    At the start the 15 past frames are real. But each frame it draws becomes part of the past. After 15 frames, the whole past is its own work.

  3. One drawing looks the same as the real frame

    Real frame 8 and the model's drawing look alike. The difference, times 8, shows only a few bright pixels. The mean miss is under one level out of 255.

    0.47mean miss, out of 255
  4. Small misses pile up

    The next frame is drawn from a slightly wrong past. Its own miss adds to the old one. So the bird height miss grows with every 100 frames of play.

    0.70 to 6.2px, step 14,169
The model never practised on its own mistakes. Stage 2 fixes that: it puts the model's own drawings into the past during training. Idea from: GameNGen (Valevski et al., 2024), the model drifts when it plays on its own frames.
Chapter K2 Stage 1 reads a real past. Stage 2 lets the model read its own drawings.

What exactly does self-forcing change in training?

  1. Start from one real window

    This is one real window of 16 frames with its keys. Stage 1 uses it as it is. Stage 2 begins with the same window.

  2. The EMA redraws two frames

    We pick s0 between 1 and 14. Here s0 is 8. The EMA reads frames before 8 and draws frame 8. Then it draws frame 9. It uses 4 passes and no gradient.

  3. Only the clean copy changes

    The clean copy is the past. Its frames 8 and 9 are now the EMA's drawings. The noisy copy and the targets stay real. So the model must still draw the real frame.

  4. Two code changes

    In loss.py the clean copy reads xc instead of x. In loop.py the EMA fills xc. The EMA only draws the past. The target stays the real frame, so nothing is copied from the EMA.

  5. The settings change too

    Stage 2 starts from the stage-1 EMA, not from random numbers. The learning rate halves and the warmup is shorter. The bird counts five times in the loss.

Same loss, same real targets, a different past. The model now learns to draw correctly even when its past is slightly wrong. Idea from: Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025), train on the model's own drawings as the past.
Chapter K3 The loss averages over every pixel. The bird covers almost none of them.

Why does the bird need five times the weight?

  1. The bird is a speck

    This frame has 16,384 pixels. The bird is only 14 orange pixels, under 0.1% of the frame. A model can miss the bird and still have a tiny loss.

  2. Find the bird pixels

    We zoom into 28 by 28 pixels around the bird. Each square is one pixel with its real colour. The black squares pass the orange test from rollout.py.

  3. Grow the mask by 3 pixels

    The bird edge and the sky next to it matter too. So bird_mask grows the orange pixels by 3 pixels each way. The mask now covers 141 pixels.

  4. Count the bird five times

    Each miss is multiplied by 1 plus 4 times the mask. So a miss near the bird counts five times. The bird share of the loss rises from 0.86% to about 4%.

    0.86%of the pixels
    5xweight on them
The weight does not change the targets. It only makes the bird's misses louder, so the model stops ignoring the bird. Idea: standard practice (weighted loss).
Chapter K4 Stage 2 ran for 120 minutes. We checked four checkpoints, not only the last.

Did stage 2 fix the bird, and what did it cost?

  1. Five numbers on five checkpoints

    Grey is our stage 1. The next four bars are stage 2 after 2,581, 5,501, 11,348 and 17,181 steps. Green means better than stage 1. Red means worse.

  2. The final checkpoint, in one line

    Survival goes from 118 to 196 frames. Wall frames drop from 0.84% to 0.006%. The bird is found in 18% of frames 101-200, up from 6%. Bird miss counts only frames where both birds are found.

    118 to 196survival, frames
    6% to 18%bird found
  3. The last checkpoint is not always the best

    Survival is highest at step 11,348 with 273 frames. Walls are lowest at the end. With one run and 32 dreams, small gaps may be noise.

  4. The dreams are real

    In these free dreams the bird stays for the frames shown. The four saved dreams last 949, 300, 895 and 41 frames. The loss would never tell us this.

  5. The cost: new pipes dip

    New pipes appear 80% of the time, down from 84%. Stage 2 is lower at every start: by 1.1, 5.1 and 4.3 points. Stage 3 targets this dip.

    84% to 80%new pipe after 4 own frames
Stage 2 helps the bird and the walls, and costs new pipes. It gains survival and bird, and it loses 4 points on pipe births. Idea from: Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025), train on the model's own drawings.
Chapter K5 Stage 2 lost some new pipes. Stage 3 practises exactly that moment.

How does stage 3 practise the moment a pipe is born?

  1. A birth window

    A birth window is 16 real frames. Its last frame is the first frame with a new pipe at the right edge. We find 7,162 of them in the training games.

  2. The test is plain pixel counting

    In frame 14 the right edge has no green. In frame 15 it has green. Check B picks its moments with the same rule.

    0green px, frame 14
    89green px, frame 15
  3. Show them 25% of the time

    Birth windows are 2.60% of all windows. Stage 3 uses them in 25% of the batches. So the model sees a pipe being born about 10 times more often.

  4. Redraw the two frames before the birth

    In a birth window s0 is 13. The EMA redraws frames 13 and 14. Then the model must draw the real frame 15, with its new pipe, from that past.

  5. Four changed lines

    The loop chooses a pool of windows with probability 0.25. In birth windows it sets s0 to 13. The loss and the bird weight stay as in stage 2.

Stage 3 is stage 2 with one change: it practises where it fails. After two of its own frames, the new pipe must still appear. Idea: ours (hard-example sampling, standard practice).
Chapter K6 The five numbers for stage 1, stage 2 and stage 3, side by side.

What did stages 2 and 3 win, and what is still open?

  1. Stage 1 is the base

    These are the five numbers of stage 1. Every other cell is coloured against them. Green means better than stage 1. Red means worse.

  2. Stage 2: walls, survival and bird

    Stage 2 cuts wall frames to 0.006% and lifts survival to 195.5. The bird miss and bird found also improve. Bird miss counts only frames where both birds are found. But new pipes drop from 84.4% to 80.1%.

  3. Stage 3: the pipes come back

    New pipes appear 97.3% of the time. Survival is 201.5 frames, the best of the three final models. Stage 2 at step 11,348 reached 273. Against stage 2, walls rise to 0.12% and bird found falls to 16%.

    97.3%new pipe, was 84.4%
    201.5survival, was 118
  4. The dreams, once more

    These are stage 3 dreams. In dream 1 the bird is lost at frame 80. In dream 2 it stays past frame 500. The median over 32 dreams is 201.5 frames.

  5. Open weights, and what is open

    All three stages are public at huggingface.co/Prahaladha/flappy-world-model. The bird in long real-key runs is still lost too often.

Stage 3 is best of the three final models on pipes (97.3%) and survival (201.5). It trades some walls and bird found against stage 2, and the weights are open to check. Idea from: Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025) for stage 2; the birth windows of stage 3 are ours.
